# Objective

Every lab in this course took one crutch away. **Lab 4** gave you an A/B
dataset and asked for a decision. **Lab 5** took away blind faith in the
criterion — you learned to validate it with Monte Carlo. **Lab 6** took away
"the data is probably normal". **Lab 7** took away the tidy chi-square line.
**Lab 8** took away the mean. **Lab 9 takes away the last one: someone else's
decision layer.** This time nobody hands you the threshold, the test, or the
verdict template. You are the lead analyst, and the memo that ships or kills
the feature carries **your** signature.

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## This is the course finale — it is worth **16 points** (double weight)

Lab 9 is the capstone: it uses every habit the course built — shape
forensics, building your own tool step by step, Monte-Carlo validation,
design-before-launch, and the decision layer. Budget your time accordingly:
this is two labs' worth of work and two labs' worth of points.
:::

**The story.** The "Free delivery on orders over 300 UAH" feature you met in
Practice 9 performed well in Kyiv, and GreenBowl is now rolling it out city
by city. You have been handed the two-week A/B experiment for **your own
city** (pulled live from `greenbowl_boot.py`, keyed to your student id).
For every user the platform logged their **total revenue over the two weeks
(2-week ARPU, UAH)** — a zero for everyone who ordered nothing, a long right
tail for the users who ordered a lot.

Finance did the math once for the whole rollout: the delivery subsidy costs
**≈3% of revenue**, so in every city the feature pays off only if it lifts
ARPU by **more than +3%** — the **breakeven**. Experiments across the rollout
are *planned* to reliably catch a **+5%** effect — the **design-MDE**. The
CFO reads one line per city: *"by how many percent did revenue grow, and
does the feature pay for itself?"*

The platform's automated report answers a different question. Its headline
is a **Welch t-test against zero** plus a **"percent CI"** made by dividing
the UAH-difference CI by the frozen control mean — the exact two traps
Practice 9 exposed: *significant ≠ profitable*, and *the denominator is a
random variable too*. Your job is to put that headline on trial, rebuild the
honest pipeline from the practice — `uplift_ci` → `uplift_ci_pois` →
`rate_uplift` → `power_sim` → `ab_report` — and deliver the memo the CFO can
actually act on.

You will:

1. Pull your experiment and print the platform's **naive headline** — the
   verdict you are about to put on trial.
2. Run **revenue forensics**: zeros, skew, and whether a handful of users
   holds a suspicious share of an arm's revenue.
3. Build the **honest uplift engine** — the ratio computed *whole* inside
   every bootstrap iteration — and compare it with the naive %-CI on your
   own data.
4. Rebuild it as a **Poisson (weighted) engine** — the way industry ships
   the bootstrap to production — prove the two engines agree, time them
   honestly, and then compute a **country-scale readout** that the classic
   engine cannot touch at any speed.
5. **Earn the right to trust your engine**: a Monte-Carlo A/A bench on data
   shaped like yours, plus the power your sample size actually had.
6. Assemble the **decision layer**: three zones against breakeven,
   P(profitable), and expected value in UAH per year.
7. **Design the next step** your verdict demands — extra weeks, a relaunch
   size, or a robustness statement — by simulation, never by formulaless
   hope.
8. Sign a one-page **go/no-go memo** to a non-technical CFO.

# General Requirements

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## The fixed business context (same for everyone)

- **Unit:** one user.
- **Metric:** **2-week ARPU, UAH** — total revenue per user over the two
  weeks, *zeros included*; higher = better.
- **Arms:** `control` = old delivery pricing, `test` = free delivery over
  300 UAH.
- **Breakeven:** the subsidy costs ~3% of revenue → the feature pays off
  only if ARPU uplift **> +3%** (`BREAKEVEN`). This is the **decision**
  threshold — the CI is compared to it *after* the experiment.
- **Design-MDE:** rollout experiments are sized to reliably catch **+5%**
  (`DESIGN_MDE`). This is the **planning** threshold — it sets $n$ *before*
  the experiment. **Do not confuse the two** (Practice 9, Part IV).
- **Scale:** `exp.user_base` is your city's user base;
  `exp.annual_revenue` = user base × control ARPU × 26 — the number that
  turns a percent into money.
- **Significance level:** $\alpha = 0.05$.
:::

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Everyone's experiment is different — on purpose

Your experiment is unique to your id. It might be a clean profitable win, a
feature that actively burns money, a result stuck between "significant" and
"profitable", a country-scale sample where significance is guaranteed and
worthless, an "uplift" manufactured by a handful of enormous accounts, or an
experiment too small to answer the question it was asked. **There is no
single "right answer" shared across the class** — there is only the memo
your pipeline supports. Copying another student's conclusion will be
obviously wrong for your city.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon="false"}

each version **reusing** the previous one. You may start from your Practice

or any library bootstrap/power/A-A function for the pipeline itself — the

# Tasks

## Get Your Experiment {#sec-data}

Download `greenbowl_boot.py` (provided with the lab) into your working
folder and load **your** experiment. Use **one** id consistently — your KSE
email is recommended.

```{python}
#| label: load
#| eval: false

from greenbowl_boot import load_my_experiment, ALPHA, BREAKEVEN, DESIGN_MDE
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportion_confint

STUDENT_ID = "your.email@kse.org.ua"   # <-- put YOUR id here
exp = load_my_experiment(STUDENT_ID)

print(exp)                     # city, arm sizes, user base
print(exp.data.head())         # one row per user: user_id, arm, revenue
control, test = exp.control, exp.test
print(f"annual revenue at stake: {exp.annual_revenue/1e6:.0f} M UAH")
```

Then run the **platform headline** — the automated report every city manager
sees. This is the verdict you are about to put on trial; do not believe it
yet.

```{python}
#| label: headline
#| eval: false

# --- the platform's automated headline (as-is, warts and all) -------------
t_stat, p = ttest_ind(test, control, equal_var=False)
d_hat = test.mean() - control.mean()
se = np.sqrt(test.var(ddof=1)/test.size + control.var(ddof=1)/control.size)
naive = (d_hat - 1.96*se) / control.mean(), (d_hat + 1.96*se) / control.mean()

print(f"ARPU uplift: {d_hat/control.mean():+.2%}   "
      f"'95% CI': ({naive[0]:+.2%}, {naive[1]:+.2%})   p = {p:.3g}")
print("HEADLINE:",
      "SHIP — significant uplift" if p < ALPHA and d_hat > 0 else
      "ROLL BACK — significant drop" if p < ALPHA else
      "DON'T SHIP — no significant uplift")
```

::: {.border}
1. State your `STUDENT_ID`. Report your **city**, $n_{\text{control}}$,
   $n_{\text{test}}$, ARPU per arm, the share of zero-revenue users per arm,
   and `annual_revenue`.
2. Run the headline and write down its verdict **verbatim**.
3. In two sentences, name the two statistical sins the headline commits
   *even before you look at the data* (hint: what is it compared against,
   and what does it pretend to know exactly?).
:::

## Revenue Forensics {#sec-shape}

Before trusting any engine, look at what the metric is made of. Revenue
data has two standard pathologies: a **mass of zeros + a long right tail**
(which you expect and the bootstrap handles), and **concentration** — a few
users so large that the arm's mean belongs to them, not to the city (which
no resampling trick can fix: the CI's promise rests on $\widehat F \approx
F$, and a tail your sample barely touches breaks it — the lecture's
edge-statistic warning in A/B costume).

::: {.border}
1. Plot both arms' revenue distributions (overlaid histograms; a log-x or a
   "positives only" view is fine as a companion). Report per arm: zero
   share, mean, median, P90, max.
2. **Concentration check:** for each arm compute the share of the arm's
   total revenue held by its **top-1** and **top-5** users. In a healthy
   arm of thousands of users these are on the order of a fraction of a
   percent to ~1–2%. Report all four numbers.
3. In one sentence: given this shape, what could make a **mean-based
   percent verdict** lie for your data — and which robust summaries
   (median uplift, winsorised mean, share of payers) would you check
   against it?
:::

::: {.callout-tip icon="false"}
## Research hook
Most students will find an unremarkable concentration profile — and that
finding is worth one sentence, not zero: "top-5 users hold X% of each arm,
the mean is not hostage to anyone." For a few of you this check will become
**the heart of the entire lab**. Skipping it and shipping a verdict you
cannot defend is the single most expensive mistake here.
:::

## The Honest Engine: `uplift_ci` {#sec-engine}

The CFO's question is **relative**: $\text{uplift} = \theta_T/\theta_C - 1$,
a statistic where both the numerator and the denominator are random. There
is no textbook CI for it — but you own the universal recipe: compute the
statistic **as a whole** on every pair of bootstrap resamples (drawn
**within** each arm, independently), and assemble the central CI
$\big(2\widehat\theta - \theta^*_{[1-\alpha/2]},\,
2\widehat\theta - \theta^*_{[\alpha/2]}\big)$.

::: {.border}
1. Implement **Version 1**, `uplift_ci(control, test, stat=np.mean,
   alpha=0.05, B=4000, seed=...)`, returning the point uplift, the central
   CI, and the array of bootstrap uplifts (`star`) — you will need the
   whole distribution later. Resample **within** each arm; compute the
   ratio **inside** every iteration.
2. Run it on your data and plot the bootstrap distribution of uplift$^*$
   with three vertical marks: zero, `BREAKEVEN`, and your CI. Describe the
   distribution's *shape* in one sentence — smooth and symmetric, skewed,
   or lumpy/multimodal — and say what a lumpy shape would tell you about
   your data (connect to @sec-shape).
3. Put the honest CI **next to the headline's naive %-CI** from @sec-data.
   If they roughly agree, say why the small-effect regime makes the naive
   version lucky (Practice 9, Part I). If they disagree — especially at the
   **lower bound**, the line the business reads — explain mechanically
   which of the headline's two sins did the damage.
4. **A/A sanity check:** split your *control* arm in half at random (fresh
   seed), run `uplift_ci` on the two halves, and confirm the CI covers
   zero. One line: why is this a necessary-but-not-sufficient check?
:::

## The Industrial Engine: `uplift_ci_pois` {#sec-pois}

GreenBowl's data platform computes metrics in a sharded warehouse — and
while your city ran its two-week test, the same feature ran as a parallel
**country-wide** experiment whose log no laptop can analyse the classic
way. Rewrite the engine with **Poisson weights**: every user gets an
independent weight $W_i \sim \text{Pois}(1)$, and the weighted mean
$(w \cdot x)/\sum w$ is computed from **sums only** — one pass over the
data, no shared state between rows.

::: {.border}
1. Implement **Version 2**, `uplift_ci_pois(control, test, alpha=0.05,
   B=4000, seed=...)`, reusing the same central-CI assembly. Report the
   share of weights $W = 0$ next to the number the lecture predicts for it.
2. Show that the Poisson CI and the classic CI from @sec-engine practically
   coincide on your data (or on a fixed-seed subsample if your city is too
   large for the classic matrix — do the arithmetic from item 4 of the
   country readout first).
3. **Time both engines honestly** on the same data, same $B$, same machine
   (`time.perf_counter`, a couple of repeats). Report both wall-clocks and
   answer plainly: is the Poisson engine faster *here*? (Expect: **no** —
   drawing $B \times N$ Poisson weights is no cheaper than drawing
   $B \times N$ indices.) One sentence: if it buys no speed on a laptop,
   what exactly are we buying it for? Your answer is the next sub-section.
:::

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Poisson is not a speed trick
On one machine, over data that fits in memory, the Poisson bootstrap is
**not faster** than the classic one — your own timer just proved it. Its
value is structural: the statistic decomposes into **per-row sums**, so it
needs (a) **O(B) memory** — accumulators instead of a $B \times N$ matrix,
(b) **one pass** — no going back to the data, and (c) **no coordination
between rows** — every shard of a distributed store can weight its own rows
independently. The classic engine needs *global random access to all rows
at once*, which is exactly what a sharded warehouse does not offer. You are
about to feel all three.
:::

### The country readout: `uplift_ci_stream`

The national experiment is served by the warehouse API — **one shard at a
time**, per its contract (see the `CountryStream` docstring):

```{python}
#| label: country
#| eval: false

from greenbowl_boot import load_country_stream

stream = load_country_stream(STUDENT_ID)
print(stream)                    # ~24 shards, ~1.2M users per arm in total
c0, t0 = stream.shard(0)         # one shard: ~50k per arm
```

::: {.callout-warning icon="false"}
## The warehouse contract
Your code may hold **one shard plus O(B) accumulators** at any moment —
never the concatenated dataset. Pretend each shard sits on its own machine:
at true warehouse scale even the raw concatenation would not fit, and the
export API simply does not offer it. Concatenating the shards into one
array voids this section.
:::

::: {.border}
1. **Arithmetic first, allocation never.** At the country's $N$ and your
   city's $B = 4000$: how many **GB** is the classic $(B, N)$ resample
   matrix per arm? And even without that matrix — why does classic
   resampling (`rng.choice` over all users) *structurally* require what the
   warehouse refuses to export? Conclude in one sentence why the classic
   engine has no path here at any speed.
2. Implement **Version 2b**, `uplift_ci_stream(stream, alpha=0.05, B=800,
   seed=...)` — one pass over the shards. For each shard $s$, draw its
   Poisson weights from a generator seeded by **`(seed, s)`** (industry
   does `hash(user_id, b)`; per-shard seeding is the same idea in
   miniature) and update four length-$B$ accumulators: $S_T[b] \mathrel{+}=
   w \cdot t$, $W_T[b] \mathrel{+}= \sum w$, and likewise for control.
   After the pass: $\text{uplift}^*_b = (S_T[b]/W_T[b])\,/\,(S_C[b]/W_C[b])
   - 1$, then the same central-CI assembly you already own. State your
   peak memory in words: one shard + four arrays of length $B$.
3. Run it on the country. Report the national uplift, its 95% CI, the
   wall-clock, and the throughput in rows/second — next to your city
   timings from item 3 above: **how many times more data did you just
   process, and in what memory footprint?** One sentence reading the national CI
   against `BREAKEVEN` (the decision drama stays with your city — this is
   the engineering readout HQ asked for).
4. **The shard-independence demo.** Process the shards in **reverse
   order** (`for i in reversed(range(stream.n_shards))`) and show the CI is
   **identical in every printed digit**. Explain why: each shard's weights
   depend only on `(seed, shard)`, so any shard can be processed on any
   machine, in any order, and the reducer just adds sums. (If you diff the
   raw floats you will find a residue around the 13th significant digit —
   that is the *order of float additions*, not statistics; saying so is
   worth a sentence.) And one more sentence: why can the classic bootstrap
   not even *state* this order-independence property?
5. To an engineer colleague, one paragraph: why does your
   `uplift_ci_stream` translate line-for-line into a SQL `GROUP BY` over
   shards? And which statistics does the one-pass trick **not** cover
   (Practice 9's limitation), and what does industry use instead?
:::

## Earn the Right to Trust It: `rate_uplift` {#sec-mc}

You deviated from the lecture's straight path twice — a ratio statistic and
Poisson weights — and the course-long habit applies: **no criterion is
trusted until Monte Carlo says it keeps its promise on data shaped like
yours, at your $n$.** In Practice 9 the bench generated worlds from the
known ARPU law. You do not know your city's law — so **fit a generator to
your control arm**: a zero with probability equal to your observed zero
share, and a lognormal fitted to the positive revenues (match the median
and the log-scale spread). That is the plug-in principle doing double duty.

::: {.border}
1. Build the generator `city_world(n, rng, uplift=0.0)` fitted to *your*
   control arm as described. Show one overlaid histogram (your control vs
   one simulated sample) as a visual goodness check — after Lab 6 you know
   better than to skip it.
2. Implement **Version 3**, `rate_uplift(engine, n, uplift=0.0, ...)` — your
   own loop: simulate A/A worlds at **your** arm sizes, count how often the
   engine's CI excludes zero, report the FPR **with a Wilson CI**. Run it
   for `uplift_ci_pois`. Is $\alpha$ inside?
3. Same bench with `uplift = DESIGN_MDE`: what **power** did your
   experiment have, at *its actual size*, against the effect the rollout
   was designed to catch? Report it with a Wilson CI.
4. One sentence interpreting item 3 for your verdict: if your CI turns out
   wide or your result "not significant", is that surprising — or exactly
   what this power figure predicts?
:::

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Match the bench to *your* data
A generic copy of the practice's bench (its ARPU constants, its n = 1500)
validates *someone else's* experiment. The FPR must be measured at **your**
arm sizes on a generator that mimics **your** control — zeros and tail
included. If your forensics found extreme concentration, say honestly
whether your fitted lognormal reproduces it, and what that means for the
bench's verdict.

## The Decision Layer: `ab_report` {#sec-decision}

Significance against **zero** is the wrong threshold: money is compared to
**breakeven**. And a binary "above/below" throws away half the information.
Assemble the final tool exactly as the practice built it: **three zones**
against `BREAKEVEN` (SHIP if the whole CI is above it, KILL if the whole CI
is below it, GREY ZONE otherwise), the **probability of profitability**
$P(\text{uplift}^* \ge \text{breakeven})$ read off the bootstrap
distribution, and the **expected value**
$EV = \text{annual\_revenue} \times (\overline{\text{uplift}^*} -
\text{breakeven})$.

::: {.border}
1. Implement **Version 4**, `ab_report(control, test, breakeven,
   annual_revenue, ...)`, **reusing** `uplift_ci_pois`. It must print:
   uplift, CI, the three-zone decision, P(profitable), and EV per year in
   UAH — and return them.
2. Run it on your experiment with `BREAKEVEN` and `exp.annual_revenue`.
   Read the report **as a whole** in 2–3 sentences: not just the zone, but
   what P(profitable) and EV add to it.
3. **Sensitivity to the economics.** Finance's 3% subsidy estimate carries
   uncertainty. Re-run at breakeven **+2%** and **+4%** (one percentage
   point either side) and state whether your zone survives. A decision that
   flips inside finance's error bars is a different memo than one that
   doesn't — say which you hold.
4. **Robustness gate.** If — and only if — your @sec-shape concentration
   check found that a handful of users holds an outsized share of an arm's
   revenue, the mean-based report above is **not allowed to stand alone**.
   Add: (a) the uplift of the **median** (via `uplift_ci` with
   `stat=np.median`); (b) the mean uplift with both arms **winsorised at
   their own P99**; (c) the mean uplift with the top handful of users
   removed, stating how many you removed. If the three robust reads and the
   mean disagree, the story of your lab is *why* — and your memo's verdict
   must follow the read you can defend, not the largest number.
:::

::: {.callout-important icon="false"}
## Stop-the-line rule
If your report compares the CI to **zero** and prints "ship" — everything
downstream is void. Zero is the threshold for "does an effect exist";
**breakeven** is the threshold for "should we pay for it". The course has
shown you enough experiments that are real-but-worthless and
grey-but-valuable; the final memo must not confuse the two.
:::

## Design the Next Step: `power_sim` {#sec-design}

A verdict is not a memo until it says **what happens next** — and "run it a
bit longer" is a gut feeling, not a plan. The tool: **power by simulation**
on a pilot. Resample your own data as the "world", inject a known uplift,
and measure how often your engine catches it.

::: {.border}
1. Implement **Version 5**, `power_sim(pilot, uplift, n, ...)`, reusing
   `uplift_ci_pois`, with your **control arm as the pilot**.
2. Follow the branch your @sec-decision zone dictates — and answer that
   branch's question **with numbers from `power_sim`**:
   - **GREY ZONE** → how many users per arm does a decisive experiment
     need (the CI must clear or exclude breakeven), and how many extra
     weeks is that at your city's enrollment rate? Assume the experiment
     enrolls new users at the two-week rate implied by your current arm
     sizes.
   - **CI too wide to say anything** (covers zero *and* breakeven with
     room to spare) → what a-priori power did this launch have at
     `DESIGN_MDE` (you already have it from @sec-mc — quote it), what $n$
     per arm would a **relaunch** need for 80% power, and should the
     original launch have happened at all?
   - **Clear SHIP or clear KILL** → your decision looks safe; prove it is
     not fragile. What is the smallest uplift your actual $n$ catches with
     ~80% power (the MDE *at your n*)? Is your observed effect comfortably
     inside that detection range, and does the zone survive the
     @sec-decision sensitivity check?
3. Whatever the branch: state the cost of your recommendation in plain
   units — weeks of experimentation, users exposed, or UAH of expected
   value forgone by waiting.
:::

::: {.callout-warning icon="false"}
## Post-hoc power is banned by name
Any line of the form *"the power at our observed effect was only X%, so the
effect is probably real"* voids this section. As Practice 9 proved, "power
at the observed effect" is a deterministic function of the p-value — zero
new information, dressed as an excuse. Power is computed **before** a
launch (or for the *next* one) on a pilot, at a **design** effect size —
never on the observed result.
:::

## The Final Memo {#sec-final}

::: {.border}
Write a **single-page memo** (≤ 400 words) to the **non-technical** CFO who
has only seen the platform's headline. It must contain:

1. The **headline verdict** (quoted) and your **one-line sign-off** — one
   of: *ship — profitability is proven*; *kill — the feature loses money*;
   *kill — the effect is real but cannot pay for its subsidy*; *extend — the
   effect is real, profitability is unproven; here is exactly how much more
   data decides it*; *don't trust the ARPU verdict — the "uplift" belongs to
   a handful of accounts; here is the metric to use instead*; or *no
   conclusion — this experiment could never answer the question; here is
   the relaunch that can*.
2. The **evidence** that forces it, quoted as numbers, not adjectives: the
   honest uplift and CI against **breakeven** (not zero), P(profitable),
   EV in UAH per year, the FPR/power of your engine at your $n$, the
   robust reads where relevant, and the `power_sim` sizing of whatever you
   recommend next.
3. A concrete **recommendation with a price tag**: what to do, how long it
   takes or what it costs, and what number will settle it.
4. One honest **caveat** of your own audit (e.g. the bench's generator is a
   fit, not the truth; a winsorised metric answers a slightly different
   question; simulation noise at your `n_exps`; the EV line assumes the
   two-week effect persists for a year).

It must be readable by someone who has never heard the words "bootstrap"
or "p-value". You are graded on whether the CFO could sign it without
follow-up questions.
:::

## Grading Details

**Correctness of methodology (6 pts):**

- `uplift_ci` is honest: resampling **within** arms, the ratio computed
  **whole** inside every iteration, the central-CI assembly correct; the
  naive-vs-honest comparison is run and explained (1.5 pt).
- `uplift_ci_pois` is correct (weights, sums-only mean, $W=0$ share
  checked, both engines timed honestly) **and** the country readout works:
  a one-pass `uplift_ci_stream` under the warehouse contract, with
  per-`(seed, shard)` weight seeding and the reverse-order identity check
  shown (1.5 pt).
- The Monte-Carlo bench is your own loop, fitted to **your** control (zeros
  + tail), run at **your** arm sizes, and reports FPR *and* power at
  `DESIGN_MDE` with Wilson CIs (1.5 pt).
- All design questions are answered by `power_sim` on a pilot; no post-hoc
  power anywhere; breakeven and design-MDE are never conflated (1.5 pt).

**Interpretation of results (6 pts):**

- @sec-shape actually **gates** the analysis: a concentration finding
  triggers the robustness reads and changes which number the memo trusts —
  not just adds a sentence (1.5 pt).
- The decision is read against **breakeven** in three zones, with
  P(profitable) and EV interpreted correctly, and the sensitivity check is
  drawn into the conclusion (1.5 pt).
- The next-step branch matches the zone and is **quantified** (users,
  weeks, UAH) — the memo never says "collect more data" without a number
  (1.5 pt).
- The memo's verdict **matches the evidence**, overturns or confirms the
  headline for the right reason, and the caveat is real, not decorative
  (1.5 pt).

**Code quality and organization (4 pts):**

- One toolkit built step by step (`uplift_ci` → `uplift_ci_pois` →
  `rate_uplift` → `power_sim` → `ab_report`), each version **reusing** the
  previous — no re-implementations inline (1.5 pt).
- Plots carry axis labels, titles, legends, and the reference lines that
  matter (zero, breakeven, $\alpha$, the 80% power target) (1.5 pt).
- Narrative precedes every code block; each section reads as an argument,
  not a dump of outputs; seeds make the report reproducible (1 pt).
:::

# Defense {.unnumbered}

During the defense (5–7 minutes) you will be asked *"What if?"* questions
that probe whether you understand **why** each piece exists, for example:

- *"Your naive and honest lower bounds differ by two percentage points.
  Show me — in your own bootstrap code — where the denominator's randomness
  enters, and what freezing it would delete."*
- *"Your CI straddles breakeven and P(profitable) is 84%. The CFO says
  'so it's probably fine — ship it.' What do you answer, and what single
  number would change your mind?"*
- *"Delete the largest user in your test arm, live, and re-run `ab_report`.
  What moved, what didn't, and what does that say about your memo?"*
- *"A city manager says: 'the test was underpowered at the observed +4%,
  so the effect is surely real, we just couldn't see it.' Respond in two
  sentences."*
- *"Your laptop has 8 GB of RAM and the national log is 40 GB across 24
  shards. Walk me through — accumulator by accumulator — how your
  `uplift_ci_stream` produces the CI, and what exactly you would ship to
  each shard's worker in a real warehouse."*
- *"Your own timer showed the Poisson engine is no faster than the classic
  one on your city. Why did you still use it for `ab_report`, and what
  breaks if the metric is the median basket instead of ARPU?"*
- *"Finance revises the subsidy: breakeven is +5%, not +3%. Re-run the
  report live and give me the new memo in one sentence."*
- *"Your A/A bench shows FPR = 9% with a Wilson CI of (6%, 13%). Which of
  your report's numbers does that poison, and what do you do next?"*
- *"You recommend four more weeks. What exactly did you simulate to get
  that number, and why is resampling your own experiment a legitimate
  stand-in for the city?"*

You may also be asked to **change one thing live** (swap the statistic to
the median, winsorise an arm, move breakeven, shrink `B`, re-seed the
bench) and explain the resulting shift.
